title: Healthcare Provider Guide to Medical Interpreter Services
summary: A practical guide to medical interpreter services for healthcare providers, including when to use an interpreter, how to speak, medications, consent, teach-back, and documentation.
body_markdown:
###


Use a medical interpreter when a patient cannot comfortably understand or discuss the clinical encounter in the provider's language. Do not rely only on conversational English ability when the visit includes symptoms, medications, risks, consent, or discharge instructions.


###


Speak directly to the patient in the first person, use complete and manageable turns, pause for interpretation, avoid overlapping speakers, and state numbers and medication details clearly.


###


Family can participate in the visit, but a qualified interpreter should usually carry the clinical interpretation. Family interpretation can filter sensitive information or change the meaning that reaches either speaker.


###


Yes, when the clinician has enough language proficiency for the clinical task and the organization's process supports direct language-concordant care. Bring in an interpreter when the conversation exceeds the clinician's language ability.


###


Yes. AI medical interpretation can support real-time spoken communication when the product is designed and tested for clinical use. Providers should still clarify uncertain turns and use human support when patient preference, policy, accessibility needs, or communication problems call for it.
